t: Lexicographically Largest String From the Box II — Maximum Bounded Suffix
o: Splitting `word` into `numFriends` non-empty parts means some piece is a suffix starting at index i, where the remaining i characters must cover the other `numFriends − 1` parts, so i ≤ n − numFriends. Every candidate string put in the box is a substring of some piece, hence a substring of one of these suffixes; conversely the whole suffix itself is achievable (pad the left side with single characters). Therefore the answer is the lexicographically largest suffix word[i:] over all valid i ∈ [0, n − numFriends]. Example: "dbca", k=2 → valid starts 0..2, largest suffix is "dbc". For "gggg" with 4 friends, only start 0 is valid, giving "g".
k: The answer is always a suffix word[i:] with i ≤ n − numFriends.
Any substring of a valid piece is dominated by the full suffix containing it.
The maximum-suffix problem has a classic amortized O(n) two-pointer solution.

a.i: Keep the best start index and compare each candidate suffix against it using native string comparison. Early mismatches make this fast on random data, though adversarial inputs like "aaaa…" degrade to quadratic.
s: Let m = n − numFriends be the largest allowed start.
Scan i from 1 to m; if word[i:] > word[best:], update best.
a.t: O(n²) worst case (e.g., all-equal characters force full-length comparisons); fast in practice due to early exits.
a.sp: O(n) for the returned substring / slices.

a.i: Maintain the current best start `b` and a match length `t`. For each new start i, compare word[i+t] with word[b+t]: if larger, i becomes the new best; if smaller, i can never beat b later in a useful way and we reset t; if equal, extend t. Each character participates in O(1) amortized comparisons, giving linear time even on highly repetitive inputs.
s: Set b = 0, t = 0; iterate i from 1 to n − numFriends.
If word[i+t] > word[b+t], set b = i, t = 0; if smaller, reset t = 0; otherwise t += 1.
a.t: O(n) — each iteration either resolves in O(1) or extends t, and t only shrinks via resets, amortizing comparisons.
a.sp: O(1) extra space besides the output.

w: Lead with the reduction to 'largest suffix among valid starts' — that insight is the whole problem. Edge cases: numFriends = 1 returns the whole word; numFriends = n returns a single character (the max character). Pitfall: allowing starts beyond n − numFriends, which would leave too few characters for the other friends. Follow-ups: the easy version (small n) allows generating all splits; suffix-array or Z-function solutions also achieve O(n log n) if asked for alternatives.
